title: Teaching Backwards From the Mind
author: Becky Allen
summary: Teaching backwards—focused remediation through dialogue rather than curriculum chunks—works fundamentally differently from initial classroom instruction. Drawing from her experience as both classroom teacher and private tutor, Becky Allen demonstrates that effective gap-filling operates outside curriculum structures entirely. The critical insight is that tutoring succeeds because it works from the student's distributed understanding of their misconception, meeting their gap on its own terms rather than routing it through predetermined curriculum sequences. Modern language models are architecturally better suited to this dialogue-based diagnostic approach than traditional adaptive learning platforms, which force errors back through curriculum-shaped pipes. The optimal remediation space lies between small conceptual holes (best served by flexible dialogue) and massive gaps (which require structured initial instruction); for the middle range, conversational AI tutoring shows promise of doubling learning impact compared to human tutoring alone.
points: Tutoring and initial classroom instruction operate through fundamentally opposite architectures: one works from the mind outward, the other imposes curriculum structure on distributed knowledge.
Error-tagged routing through pre-built curriculum lessons is inefficient remediation because gaps are idiosyncratic and rarely align with curriculum-shaped chunks.
The tutor's distributed, flexible mind directly meets the student's distributed gap without intermediary curriculum structures—no chunking required.
Language models have the right architecture to replicate tutoring dialogue rather than the localist curriculum-mapping that traditional edtech attempts.
Remediation success requires working backwards from specific, messy misconceptions rather than forwards through sequenced curriculum content.
quotes: Tutoring had none of that. A student would arrive with a question they couldn't do, and the entire session would grow outward from that question. I wasn't delivering content. I was trying to get inside their head by probing what they understood, forming hypotheses about where their thinking had gone wrong, testing those hypotheses with follow-up questions, and building a mini-explanation on the fly that was shaped entirely by what I found.

The tutor just asks. 'OK, what's an indirect tax?' The student answers correctly — fine, move on. The tutor probes further. Well, who actually pays VAT: the shopper or the business?' The student says the shopper. The tutor asks whether a business might absorb some of the increase rather than pass it all on. The student hasn't considered that. Now the tutor knows: the gap isn't about definitions or examples.

An LLM that's allowed to operate as a distributed mind could do what the tutor does. It could start from the wrong answer, probe the student's understanding through dialogue, form and test hypotheses about where the confusion lies, and build the remediation on the fly.
For the first time, we have tools with the right architecture to do remediation the way tutors actually do it. Not by finding the right pre-built chunk, but by not chunking at all.

The distributed mind does the repair work freely, meeting the student's gap on its own terms. Then you describe what happened in curriculum language: 'We worked on tracing the economic effects of indirect tax changes; the student's difficulty was with tax incidence rather than definitions.'
The question is whether we're willing to let the technology work the same way.” Archived from Substack on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
